reading.translation:
The Greeks crossed the river and began the march. They placed the baggage animals in the middle. Their enemies sent horsemen and archers.

The enemies kept shooting from a distance. The Greeks pursued them, but did not catch them. Xenophon led the soldiers back toward the army’s main body.

The other generals criticized Xenophon. On hearing, he accepted the criticism. The pursuit had not saved the soldiers; a different preparation was necessary.

Xenophon spoke about the Rhodians. These men have slings and use lead. The generals identified those able to sling and allocated money to them.

Two hundred slingers prepared themselves. The generals also gathered horses. On the next day they organized fifty horsemen; Lycius commanded the cavalry.

The Greeks made their preparations and remained. They had not yet reached the sea or arrived home. Now they prepare the route through shared deliberation.

In Memorabilia Socrates speaks about a general. A leader must care for the others. He wants not only to fare well himself, but also for those following him to fare well.

blocks.title: Skill, preparation, and care
body: σφενδόνη is a sling; σφενδονήτης is a slinger. The equipment noun and the person noun belong together, but they are not interchangeable. τοξότης names a different specialist, the archer.

παρασκευή is preparation; παρασκευάζομαι is to prepare oneself. In παρεσκευάσαντο the internal augment and first-aorist middle ending combine in one form. The reading connects preparation with specific people and equipment, not an abstract feeling of bravery.

ἐπιμελέομαι takes a genitive of the people cared for. τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιμελεῖσθαι means to care for others. This phrase bridges the retreat’s practical changes and the separate Memorabilia discussion of the commander’s responsibility.

sections.title: 1. Asigmatic first aorists: liquids and nasals
body: Verb stems ending in λ, μ, ν, or ρ often have first-aorist endings without a visible σ. Historically σ is lost and the preceding vowel is lengthened or otherwise altered. μένω gives ἔμεινα; νέμω gives ἔνειμα. These are first aorists, not second aorists merely because σ is absent.

The first-aorist ending pattern remains: ἔμεινα, ἔμεινας, ἔμεινε(ν), ἐμείναμεν, ἐμείνατε, ἔμειναν. κρίνω → ἔκρινα has a long ι in its aorist stem; ordinary Greek spelling does not mark that length. Learn stem changes with the principal parts.

Infinitive μεῖναι and participle μείνας also have no σ. Compare second-aorist λαβεῖν and λαβών. The first-aorist forms show the α-type pattern in -αι and -ας; the thematic second aorist has its distinct ο/ε pattern.

sections.title: 2. Irregular first-aorist stems and principal parts
body: The sigmatic pattern does not make every stem predictable from its present form. καίω, “burn,” forms ἔκαυσα; κλαίω, “weep,” forms ἔκλαυσα. Their αυ before σ must be learned with the principal parts, rather than generated by retaining the present -αι-.

ἀπόλλυμι, “destroy / lose,” supplies active ἀπώλεσα. This is a sigmatic first aorist with the stem ὀλεσ- and internal temporal augment after the preverb ἀπο-. Its middle aorist ἀπωλόμην, “I perished,” belongs to a different second-aorist pattern and is a supplied meaning contrast, not today’s production paradigm.

An irregular first aorist can even lack σ: φέρω has ἤνεγκα as well as second-aorist ἤνεγκον. This exceptional first-aorist stem is supplied for recognition only. The assessed irregular sigmatic forms in this section are ἔκαυσα, ἔκλαυσα, and ἀπώλεσα; no rule about “all first aorists contain σ” is valid.

sections.title: 3. Augment in compound verbs
body: In a compound verb the augment normally comes after the preverb and before the verb stem. Thus συν- + ἔλεξα becomes συνέλεξα, while παρα- + ἐσκευασάμην gives παρεσκευασάμην. The preverb keeps its directional or relational contribution to the meaning.

Preverbs ending in a vowel commonly lose that final vowel before syllabic augment: παρα- → παρ- + ἐ-, ἀπο- → ἀπ- + ἐ-. περί and πρό are notable exceptions to a universal “drop every final vowel” rule; learn each compound’s attested form. With temporal augment, ἀπο- + ὀλεσα yields ἀπώλεσα.

Consonant assimilation follows the sound immediately after a preverb. συν- becomes συμ- before β in present συμβάλλω, but the intervening augment restores ν in aorist συνέβαλον. Participles have no augment: παρασκευασάμενος and συλλέξας contrast with augmented indicatives.

checks.prompt: Where does augment normally go in a compound?
checks.answer: after the preverb. The augment precedes the verbal stem after its preverb.

checks.prompt: Which is the aorist of συλλέγω?
checks.answer: συνέλεξα. The augment intervenes after συν-.

sections.title: 4. Cumulative review: nouns, adjectives, and reference
body: Module II expanded noun systems: third-declension velar, dental, labial, nasal, liquid, and -ντ- stems; neuters in -μα; vowel stems πόλις and ἄστυ; diphthong patterns βασιλεύς, ναῦς, and βοῦς; family nouns πατήρ and μήτηρ; irregular γυνή and χείρ. A genitive reveals the stem, while gender and agreement identify the words connected in the sentence. σώφρων, σῶφρον has a common masculine/feminine form and a separate neuter; πᾶς, πᾶσα, πᾶν agrees in all three genders. The article can turn an adjective into a substantive: οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι means “the brave.”

Review the article with attributive phrases (οἱ ἐν τῷ στρατοπέδῳ στρατιῶται) and possessive or partitive genitives (τοῦ στρατηγοῦ, τινὲς τῶν στρατιωτῶν). A reflexive ἑαυτοῦ refers back to the subject; αὐτοῦ can refer to a different man. Interrogative τίς / τί has its written accent; indefinite τις / τι is normally enclitic.

Numbers and time phrases are meaningful information, not decorative morphology. πέντε στρατηγοί and εἴκοσι λοχαγοί distinguish offices and counts. τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ is dative “on the next day”; νυκτός is genitive “during the night”; τρεῖς ἡμέρας is accusative “for three days.” A genitive expression such as τριῶν ἡμερῶν can specify “within three days”; distinguish that use from the genitive period νυκτός, “during the night.”

sections.title: 5. Cumulative review: participles, futures, and narrative
body: Present active participles such as μένων and present middle πορευόμενος describe an action as ongoing. They agree with their head noun. With the article, ὁ λέγων means “the speaker / person speaking”; ὁ λέγων στρατηγός is “the general who is speaking.” A simple circumstantial λέγων can mean “while speaking.” Present participles express ongoing action relative to the main verb, not an independent calendar date. First-aorist λύσας / λυσάμενος and second-aorist λαβών / λαβόμενος view their actions as wholes, often before the main action in a narrative.

Future forms include regular sigmatic λύσω (middle λύσομαι), consonant changes such as πέμπω → πέμψω, contract-verb sigmatic τιμήσω, asigmatic -ίζω future νομιῶ from νομίζω, and liquid/nasal contract μενῶ; deponent ἔρχομαι has middle-form future ἐλεύσομαι with active meaning; εἶμι commonly has future meaning “I shall go,” contrasting with εἰμί, “I am.” Future participles such as βοηθήσων can express purpose: “intending to help.” Impersonal δεῖ and χρή combine with an infinitive to name an action required.

Put form and interpretation together: who acts, whom a participle describes, and how that action relates to the main verb. The past indicative aorist has augment, whereas participles and infinitives lack it. This cumulative section adds review to all three new Lesson 24 topics; it does not substitute review for liquid aorists, irregular sigmatic stems, or compound augment.

sections.title: A tactical failure becomes useful knowledge
body: The early retreat brings enemies who can shoot from beyond the Greeks’ effective range. An infantry pursuit fails to catch them and takes pursuers away from the main body. Xenophon receives criticism from fellow commanders and acknowledges its force.

The episode joins courage to correction. A responsible leader can accept that his response did not work, identify the actual weakness, and seek a different method. The source supports this sequence of learning; it does not make every proposal by Xenophon successful from the outset.

sections.title: Skills already present in the army
body: Rhodians in the army know how to use slings and lead projectiles. The commanders turn an existing skill into an organized force, with incentives and equipment. Horses already available are reassigned for a small cavalry unit rather than conjured from an unlimited supply.

Anabasis reports two hundred slingers organized in the night and fifty horsemen accepted the next day, with Lycius son of Polystratus commanding the cavalry. The solution is collective and material: trained people, projectiles, horses, armor, and decisions all matter.

sections.title: Bringing others through danger
body: Memorabilia 3.2 connects a commander’s role with the good condition and success of those he leads. Socrates’s argument is a separate ethical comparison. It invites us to judge leadership by care for followers as well as by the leader’s own fortune.

Across this module, Cyrus seeks a throne, Clearchus commits officers to a risky meeting, Cleocritus appeals to civic ties, and Xenophon helps reorganize survival. Use the named readings to compare their purposes and decisions. This lesson ends in improved preparation at the beginning of retreat; the sea and home remain ahead.
